title: Rof
author: Pierre Thiam
desc: The parsley, garlic, onion and scallion paste that goes into slits cut in the fish — about a teaspoon per steak, and it makes about a cup.
longDesc: Not a garnish but a structural part of ceebu jen: a coarse pounded paste of three garlic cloves, a bunch of parsley, a white onion, three scallions, a tablespoon of chilli flakes and a tablespoon of black pepper, with an optional bouillon cube. Two two-inch slits are cut in each fish steak and filled with about a teaspoon each, and the rest coats the fish including the head and tail before it rests in the fridge. The recipe makes about a cup, enough for a five-pound fish cut into seven steaks.
equipment: Mortar and pestle, or a blender
steps: Blend or pound all the ingredients to a coarse paste — not smooth.
Cut two 2-inch slits in each fish steak.
Fill each slit with about 1 teaspoon of rof.
Coat the rest of the fish with what remains, including the head and tail.
Refrigerate until you are ready to cook.
chefTips: Coarse, not smooth. A blitzed purée leaks out of the slits; a coarse paste stays put and holds its texture through the poaching.
Two slits per steak, about a teaspoon each. More than that and it falls out into the broth.
Stuff the head and tail too. They go into the pot in a proper ceebu jen and they carry a lot of the flavour.
A tablespoon each of chilli flakes and black pepper sounds like a lot for one cup — it is correct, and the fish dilutes it considerably.
Makes about a cup, which is the right amount for a five-pound fish in seven steaks. Scale with the fish, not with the rice.
Refrigerating after stuffing is part of the method, not just convenience: it lets the paste work into the flesh.
Senegalese cooks also spell it roff and build it differently — parsley with bird's eye chilli, garlic, pepper and salt is another documented version, without the onion or scallion.
commonMistakes: Leaving the head and tail unstuffed.
Using it immediately rather than letting the fish rest.
Cutting the chilli and pepper because the quantity looks high.
sources: Adapted from the rof component of 'Thiebou Jenn', published from Pierre Thiam and Jennifer Sit, 'Senegal: Modern Senegalese Recipes from the Source to the Bowl' (Lake Isle Press, 2015), via southernfoodways.org (no author byline on the page; excerpt credited to Thiam and Sit) and explorepartsunknown.com (BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Pierre Thiam'; 4 April 2017). Yield as printed on both: 'makes about 1 cup'. The two independent publications agree on the ingredient list, so it is treated as TWO-PASS by cross-publication agreement; strict verbatim transcription was refused on both domains by the retrieval layer's quote cap.

Ingredients as printed: '3 garlic cloves'; '1 bunch parsley, coarsely chopped'; '1 white onion, coarsely chopped'; '3 scallions, chopped'; '1 vegetable or fish bouillon cube (optional)'; '1 Tbsp chile flakes'; '1 Tbsp freshly ground black pepper'.
THE APPLICATION, as printed in the parent recipe: cut two 2-inch slits per steak and fill each with about 1 teaspoon of rof, then coat the fish including head and tail and refrigerate.

A SECOND DOCUMENTED FORMULA, recorded unreconciled: Aïssatou Mbaye's roff, used in her white ceebu jen, is parsley with '2 ou 3 piments oiseau', '3 gousses d'ail' and 'du poivre et un peu de sel' — no onion, no scallion, no chilli flakes. A third, from Amina Savoura's thiébou dieun, is 'un bouquet de persil frisé', '1 piment', '2 gousses d'ail', '1 cube de bouillon maggi' and 'poivre noir'. Three versions of one paste, none corrected toward another.
NOTE THAT ROF IS DISTINCT FROM ROF GREMOLATA, a separate preparation by the same author published in his later work as a finishing condiment rather than a stuffing. That one is at SEN092.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE ENTRY: five of the rice dishes in this collection call for rof by name and by the teaspoon. Publishing it once and cross-referencing it is more useful than repeating it five times, and it is a real preparation in its own right.
NO SERVING SIZE is printed. The eight servings above is an editorial division of about a cup.
storage: 2 days refrigerated in a sealed jar. It darkens but keeps.
healthBenefits: Parsley is exceptionally high in vitamin K and vitamin C.
Garlic and scallion supply organosulfur compounds.
Negligible calories, and it replaces salt as a flavour driver.
Vegan without the optional bouillon cube.
culturalNote: Stuffing the fish rather than seasoning its surface is what makes Senegalese fish cookery distinctive, and the slits-and-paste technique is the first thing a Senegalese cook teaches about ceebu jen. The paste has at least three documented formulas, which is the usual state of a thing every household makes weekly.
